blocks.md:
Why the fix works: each ECU has its own secret, so extracting one tells you nothing about the next car; the answer is an HMAC (a keyed hash), which cannot be inverted to recover the secret; the 128-bit random challenge never repeats in practice, so a recorded answer is useless; and the attempt counter turns guessing into a lockout. A stronger design keeps the secret out of the tester entirely: the tester asks the maker's backend to compute the answer for an authenticated, logged workshop user.

UDS **Authentication** (service `29`) moves to certificates. AUTOSAR's Dcm supports "verifyCertificateUnidirectional", "verifyCertificateBidirectional" and "proofOfOwnership", and notes that certificate-based access "can be limited in time or bound to certain vehicles or ECUs only". AUTOSAR implements only the certificate (PKI) variant; challenge-response authentication under service 29 is left to custom code.

**Defender view.** UN R155's Annex 5 lists "Diagnostic access (e.g. dongles in OBD port) used to facilitate an attack" (threat 18.3), with mitigation M22, security controls on external interfaces. Concretely:

- Gateways should allow diagnostic sessions only from the OBD-II path, and only while stationary, using an authenticated speed.
- Log every SecurityAccess and Authentication attempt, success or failure, as a security event (lesson 5). A burst of invalidKey responses is an attack signal.
- Treat aftermarket OBD dongles (insurance trackers, fleet devices) as a remote interface into the car: they often have their own cellular or Bluetooth link.

blocks.prompt: A maker uses a strong HMAC for sendKey but the ECU generates seeds with a 16-bit counter that resets to 0 at every power-up. What breaks?
blocks.reveal: The challenge repeats. After each power cycle the ECU issues the same sequence of seeds, so an attacker who recorded a genuine tester's sendKey for seed 0 can replay it after the next reboot. Strong MAC, weak freshness: the same failure as SecOC without a freshness check (lesson 6). Seeds must come from a random number generator with enough bits, as in the code's 128-bit challenge.

blocks.question: Why does a per-ECU secret matter more than a longer seed?
options: It makes the seed exchange faster
Extracting the secret from one ECU or one tester tool then unlocks only that ECU, not every vehicle of the model
UDS requires it for service 0x10
It removes the need for an attempt counter
blocks.explain: The scale question from the IoT threat model: a shared secret turns one extraction into a fleet-wide key. A longer seed only stops replays and brute force against one ECU.

blocks.question: An ECU returns NRC 0x37 to SecurityAccess. What does that tell the tester?
options: The delay timer after too many failed attempts has not expired
The key was wrong
The service is not supported in this session
The ECU has unlocked
blocks.explain: 0x37 is requiredTimeDelayNotExpired. 0x35 is invalidKey, 0x36 exceededNumberOfAttempts (which starts the delay), and 0x7F means the service is not supported in the active session.

lessons.title: Keys inside the ECU: SHE, HSMs and secure boot

blocks.md:
SecOC, seed-key with per-ECU secrets and signed updates all assume an ECU can keep a key secret and refuse to use it when its own code has been tampered with. The IoT course taught the general tools: a chain of trust that starts in ROM, and per-device keys in a secure element. Cars have their own standard building block for this.

Tiny example: a brake ECU holds the SecOC key for brake frames. If an attacker replaces its bootloader (the Jeep's V850, lesson 7, accepted unsigned firmware), the new code could use that key to sign anything. The goal is that modified code finds the key **locked**.

**SHE** (Secure Hardware Extension; the specification's glossary also says Security Hardware Extension) is a small security module built into automotive microcontrollers. It was specified by **HIS** (Hersteller Initiative Software; Hersteller is German for manufacturer) and is republished by AUTOSAR ([SHE functional specification](https://www.autosar.org/fileadmin/standards/R24-11/FO/AUTOSAR_FO_TR_SecureHardwareExtensions.pdf)). It is built around AES-128, with CMAC for MACs, and holds keys in fixed slots that software can use but not read.

SHE's key slots:

- **MASTER_ECU_KEY**: the owner's key, used only to update other slots.
- **BOOT_MAC_KEY** and **BOOT_MAC**: the key and stored reference MAC for secure boot.
- **KEY_1 ... KEY_n**: application keys, for example SecOC keys.

Each slot carries flags: write protection, boot protection (unusable if secure boot failed), debugger protection (disabled when a debugger is attached), key usage (encryption or MAC) and wildcard (whether a key may be updated without naming this chip's unique ID). New keys arrive through an update protocol of messages M1 to M3, authenticated with a CMAC under a key the sender must already know.

SHE's secure boot works like this. Code in the microcontroller's ROM reads the first stage of user code, the "SHE Bootloader", and pipes it to SHE, which computes its CMAC with BOOT_MAC_KEY and compares it with BOOT_MAC. On the first boot after a BOOT_MAC_KEY is written, SHE simply stores the computed MAC ("autonomous bootstrap"); after that, every boot is checked.

The important detail is what happens on a mismatch. By default SHE does **not** stop the CPU. Its "sanctions" are: set status bits that say the boot failed, and lock every key marked boot-protected. An optional mode, "Enforcing authenticated software", refuses to start non-authentic code at all, and must be configured in one-time-programmable memory so it cannot be switched off.

blocks.title: SHE secure boot: measure, compare, lock keys

scenes.caption: At reset, ROM code reads the SHE Bootloader from flash and pipes it to SHE before running it.
SHE computes CMAC(BOOT_MAC_KEY, bootloader) and compares it with BOOT_MAC. Match: boot OK, keys usable.
The application then asks SHE for SecOC MACs with KEY_1. It never sees the key itself.
A tampered bootloader: the CMAC differs. In default mode the code still runs, but boot-protected keys are locked.
The tampered ECU cannot produce valid SecOC tags, so other ECUs reject its frames. Secure boot plus SecOC turns firmware tampering into a detectable, contained failure.

blocks.code:
# SHE-style secure boot, simplified: on a BOOT_MAC mismatch the code still
# runs, but boot-protected keys lock, so it cannot sign SecOC frames.
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.cmac import CMAC
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import algorithms

def cmac(key, data):
    c = CMAC(algorithms.AES(key)); c.update(data); return c.finalize()

class She:
    def __init__(self, boot_mac_key, secoc_key):
        self.boot_mac_key = boot_mac_key
        self.boot_mac = None                      # learned on first boot
        self.keys = {"SECOC_KEY": (secoc_key, True)}   # (key, boot_protected)
        self.boot_ok = False
    def secure_boot(self, bootloader):
        m = cmac(self.boot_mac_key, bootloader)
        if self.boot_mac is None:                 # autonomous bootstrap
            self.boot_mac = m
        self.boot_ok = (m == self.boot_mac)
    def mac(self, slot, msg):
        key, protected = self.keys[slot]
        if protected and not self.boot_ok:
            return "ERROR: key locked (boot failed)"
        return cmac(key, msg)[:3].hex()

mod = She(bytes(16), bytes(range(16)))
genuine = b"bootloader v3" + bytes(100)
mod.secure_boot(genuine)                          # factory: learn BOOT_MAC
mod.secure_boot(genuine)
print("genuine boot :", mod.boot_ok, mod.mac("SECOC_KEY", b"brake 0%"))
mod.secure_boot(b"bootloader v3" + b"\x90" + bytes(99))   # one byte patched
print("patched boot :", mod.boot_ok, mod.mac("SECOC_KEY", b"brake 0%"))
blocks.caption: Toy model of SHE's default sanction: the boot completes, but boot-protected keys refuse to work.

blocks.code:
genuine boot : True a56eae
patched boot : False ERROR: key locked (boot failed)
blocks.caption: Output of the code above (a real run).

blocks.md:
ECUs that need more use a full **HSM** (hardware security module): a separate core with its own memory that also does public-key cryptography, so it can verify firmware signatures and certificates (needed for UDS service 29 and for over-the-air updates, next lesson). The principle is the same: keys stay inside, use is gated on a verified boot.

Ken Tindell, chief technology officer of Canis Automotive Labs, notes that even older ECUs without SHE hardware could run a software-emulated SHE in about 3 KB of code and 200 bytes of RAM, at about 40 microseconds per operation, but that ECUs must then be "provisioned with secret keys (typically at the factory) so that each vehicle uses different keys", and re-provisioned when an ECU is replaced or moved ([CAN injection post](https://kentindell.github.io/2023/04/03/can-injection/)). Key provisioning, not cryptography, is usually the hard part.

SHE secure boot in its default mode is a *key gate*, not a *boot blocker*. If no keys are marked boot-protected, or if the application never uses SHE keys for anything that others verify, a failed secure boot changes nothing an attacker cares about. Check which keys carry the boot protection flag.

blocks.question: An ECU's SHE reports a failed secure boot, but the ECU keeps sending frames. What prevents those frames from being trusted?
options: Nothing; SHE in default mode only sets a status bit
Boot-protected keys are locked, so the ECU cannot compute valid SecOC tags and receivers reject its authenticated frames
SHE erases the application from flash
The CAN controller refuses to transmit
blocks.explain: SHE's default sanctions set the status bits and lock boot-protected keys. Protection therefore depends on receivers verifying SecOC tags made with those keys. Erasing flash or blocking transmission is not part of the default behaviour.

blocks.question: Why does SHE disable debugger-protected keys while a debugger is attached?
options: To save power
Because JTAG uses the same pins as CAN
To speed up flashing
Because a debugger can run or alter arbitrary code, so keys must not be usable by code that was not measured at boot
blocks.explain: A debugger bypasses the boot measurement. The IoT course's debug-port lesson made the same point: locking debug access protects secrets. SHE ties key availability to that state and only re-enables the slots after a reset.

lessons.title: Over-the-air updates: UN R156 and the Uptane framework

blocks.md:
An over-the-air (OTA) update lets a maker fix a car without a workshop visit. The Jeep recall needed USB sticks mailed to owners; a car with secure OTA could have been fixed without any mailing. But an update channel that can rewrite every ECU in a fleet is the most valuable target a car maker owns.

Tiny example: a maker's update server is compromised. If cars install whatever that server signs, one breach reaches every vehicle at once. The IoT course covered signed images and anti-rollback for one device. A car adds two problems: dozens of ECUs from different suppliers that must stay mutually compatible, and an online server that must decide which car gets what.

**UN Regulation 156** (software update and software update management system) sets the legal floor ([text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/388/oj/eng/pdf)). The maker needs a certified **SUMS** (software update management system: "organizational processes and procedures" for delivering updates), and each vehicle type may carry an **RXSWIN** (RX software identification number) that identifies the type-approval-relevant software, with an "auditable register" of what belongs to each RXSWIN. For the vehicle itself:

- "The authenticity and integrity of software updates shall be protected" (7.2.1.1).
- After a failed or interrupted update, the vehicle must "restore systems to their previous version" or reach a safe state (7.2.2.1.1).
- Updates run only with enough power to finish or recover (7.2.2.1.2).
- The user is told the purpose, the expected time and which functions are unavailable (7.2.2.2), and if updating while driving is unsafe, the car cannot be driven during it (7.2.2.3).

R156 says *what*; **Uptane** is a published design for *how*. The [Uptane Standard 2.1.0](https://uptane.org/docs/latest/standard/uptane-standard) builds on The Update Framework (TUF), which it cites, and splits trust between two repositories:

- **Image repository**: holds every image and signed metadata about it (hashes, sizes, hardware identifiers). It is "primarily controlled by human actors, and updated relatively infrequently", so its signing keys can stay away from automated online servers.
- **Director repository**: "mostly controlled by automated, online processes". It reads a vehicle's report of what is installed and signs instructions saying which image each ECU should install.

Each repository has TUF's four roles: **Root** (distributes and revokes the other keys), **Targets** (signs image metadata), **Snapshot** (which Targets files go together) and **Timestamp** (signals that new metadata exists). In the car, a **Primary** ECU downloads everything and checks it; **Secondary** ECUs receive images from the Primary.

blocks.title: Uptane: two repositories must agree before an ECU installs

scenes.caption: The Image repository, run by people and updated rarely, signs what exists. The Director signs what this particular car should install, online.

The Primary performs full verification: all four roles on both repositories, then checks that the Director's chosen image matches the Image repository's entry (hash, length, hardware id, release counter).
Secondaries get images through the Primary. A Secondary that cannot do more must still do partial verification: check the time and the Director's Targets metadata for itself.
Director key stolen: the attacker can sign instructions, but the image they name must also be signed by the separately controlled Image repository. A malicious image fails the match.
The Primary reports a signed vehicle version manifest back to the Director: what each ECU runs and any attack it detected. That report is also monitoring data for the security team.

blocks.code:
import json, hashlib
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey as K

image_key, director_key = K.generate(), K.generate()  # held by separate parties
def signed(key, body):
    raw = json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()
    return {"body": body, "sig": key.sign(raw)}
def valid(pub, md):
    try: pub.verify(md["sig"], json.dumps(md["body"], sort_keys=True).encode()); return True
    except Exception: return False

def entry(blob, ctr): return {"sha256": hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest(), "hw": "brake-v2", "ctr": ctr}
v1, v2, evil = b"brake fw 1", b"brake fw 2", b"brake fw evil"
image_repo = signed(image_key, {"fw1": entry(v1, 1), "fw2": entry(v2, 2)})

def primary_check(director, ecu_hw="brake-v2", installed_ctr=2):
    if not (valid(image_key.public_key(), image_repo) and valid(director_key.public_key(), director)):
        return "REJECT: bad signature"
    name, want = director["body"]["file"], director["body"]["target"]
    have = image_repo["body"].get(name)
    if have != want: return "REJECT: Director and Image repo disagree"
    if want["hw"] != ecu_hw: return "REJECT: wrong hardware"
    if want["ctr"] < installed_ctr: return "REJECT: rollback (release counter)"
    return f"INSTALL {name}"

print(primary_check(signed(director_key, {"file": "fw2", "target": entry(v2, 2)})))
# Director's online key stolen: it can sign, but cannot change the Image repo.
print(primary_check(signed(director_key, {"file": "fw2", "target": entry(evil, 2)})))
print(primary_check(signed(director_key, {"file": "fw1", "target": entry(v1, 1)})))
blocks.caption: Toy check with Ed25519 signatures (cryptography package). Simplified: real Uptane verifies Root, Timestamp, Snapshot and Targets on both repositories, with signature thresholds.

blocks.code:
INSTALL fw2
REJECT: Director and Image repo disagree
REJECT: rollback (release counter)
blocks.caption: Output of the code above (a real run).

blocks.md:
The two rejections are the point of the design. A stolen Director key lets an attacker *choose among genuine images*, not ship new ones. And the **release counter**, which the standard recommends in the metadata both repositories must match, "can be used to prevent rollback attacks even in cases where the Director repository is compromised".

The standard's threat model names attacks worth knowing by name: **freeze** (keep sending "a properly signed, but old" bundle so the car never learns of a fix), **rollback** (install an older vulnerable version), **mix-and-match** (combine individually valid images that do not work together; Snapshot metadata defends against it), **partial bundle** (let only some ECUs update), **slow retrieval** and **endless data** (starve or flood the download), and **arbitrary software**. Timestamp metadata with an expiry is what defeats freeze: stale metadata is rejected even if correctly signed.

Split trust so that one stolen key is not enough: keys handled by people for *what is allowed to exist*, online keys for *who gets what*, and a version floor the online side cannot lower. Then make the car report what it runs.

blocks.question: An attacker steals the Director repository's online signing key. With Uptane full verification on the Primary, what can they do?
options: Install any firmware they write on any ECU
Nothing at all
Instruct ECUs to install genuine images listed in the Image repository, but not new malicious ones and not images below the release counter
Read all images in plaintext
blocks.explain: The Director's choice must match an Image repository entry signed with the Image repository's separate keys, and the release counter blocks rollback. The attacker keeps limited power (for example, withholding updates), which is why the Director's key still needs protection and monitoring.

blocks.question: A car keeps receiving correctly signed metadata, but it is three months old and lists no new versions. Which Uptane mechanism detects this freeze attack?
options: Expiring Timestamp metadata, which must be fresh to be accepted
Mix-and-match protection in Snapshot
The hardware identifier
Partial verification
blocks.explain: Signatures alone cannot show that data is current. Timestamp metadata is re-signed often with a short expiry, so a frozen copy eventually expires and the ECU knows it is being withheld updates.

lessons.title: Keyless entry: relay attacks, weak fob crypto and distance bounding

blocks.md:
Car keys became radios in stages, and each stage has its own weakness:

- **Immobiliser transponder**: a chip in the key that answers the car over low-frequency radio from a few centimetres, so the engine control unit agrees to run.
- **RKE** (remote keyless entry): the button on the fob sends a code over UHF (ultra high frequency) radio (315 or 433 MHz) with a range of 10 to 100 metres.
- **PKES** (passive keyless entry and start): you keep the key in your pocket. The car sends low-frequency (LF) beacons or challenges (the paper's relay worked at 135 kHz) with a range of about a metre; the key wakes, computes a response and answers on UHF. A valid answer opens the doors; another exchange from inside the car allows the engine to start.

These figures are from Aurelien Francillon, Boris Danev and Srdjan Capkun of ETH Zurich, NDSS 2011 ([paper](https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/franc.pdf)).

Tiny example of the flaw they named: the short LF range was the car's only evidence that the key was near. As the paper puts it, "instead of verifying that the correct key is in its physical proximity, the car verifies if it can communicate with the correct key".

A **relay attack** exploits exactly that. One device near the car picks up the LF signal and passes it over a longer link to a second device near the key, which re-emits it. The key answers; the car hears a cryptographically perfect response. The researchers stress that the relay is "completely independent of the modulation, protocol, or presence of strong authentication and encryption": nothing is decrypted or forged, the real key does all the cryptography.

What they measured, on 10 car models from 8 manufacturers: relaying only the car-to-key direction was enough; the key could be up to 50 m away, non line-of-sight; on some models the key could be woken from 8 m; and the cars tolerated added delays of 35 microseconds up to tens of milliseconds before rejecting a response. Light travels about 10.5 km in 35 microseconds, so those timeouts said nothing about distance.

blocks.title: A relay stretches the car's 1 metre LF range

scenes.caption: Normal use: the key is within about a metre, hears the LF challenge and answers on UHF. Proximity is implied by LF range alone.
Relay: device A near the car captures the LF challenge and sends it over a long-range link to device B near the key (a house, a cafe).
Device B re-emits the challenge. The genuine key computes the correct response with its genuine secret.
The key's UHF reply reaches the car directly (UHF carries tens of metres). The car verifies it: correct. Doors unlock; the same trick starts the engine.
With distance bounding the car times the exchange. The relay's cable, radio and electronics add hundreds of nanoseconds: the computed distance is far beyond 2 m. Rejected.

blocks.md: **Distance bounding** is the principled fix. The verifier sends a challenge, the prover replies, and the verifier measures the round-trip time, subtracts the prover's known processing time and converts the rest into distance at the speed of light, about 0.3 m per nanosecond. A relay can only add delay, never remove it, so, as Francillon and colleagues put it, "the attacker cannot convince them that they are closer than they really are, just further". The timing must be measured in nanoseconds; that is why modern systems use **UWB** (ultra-wideband) radio, whose very short pulses allow precise time-of-flight ranging (IEEE 802.15.4z).

blocks.title: What a time-of-flight check concludes about a relayed key

scenes.caption: Owner at 1.5 m, no relay: bound 1.5 m, under the 2 m threshold. With a 20 ns relay delay each way, even a 1 m relay link pushes the bound past 2 m.
A hypothetical relay with zero electronics delay still adds its path length: any real relay distance shows up in the bound.
Simplified model: assumes the fob's reply time is exact and the signal is measured cleanly. Ghost Peak (below) attacks the second assumption.

blocks.caption: Toy time-of-flight check. The 35 microsecond acceptance window is the smallest maximum delay Francillon and colleagues measured on a real car.

blocks.code:
owner at the door, 1.5 m   RTT    10.0 ns | bound   1.5 m | timing-blind car: open   | distance bounding: open
relay, fob 30 m away       RTT   250.1 ns | bound  37.5 m | timing-blind car: open   | distance bounding: refuse
blocks.caption: Output of the code above (a real run).

blocks.md: UWB is not magic. Patrick Leu and colleagues (ETH Zurich and TU Darmstadt) presented **Ghost Peak** at USENIX Security 2022 ([paper page](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity22/presentation/leu)): "the first over-the-air attack on IEEE 802.15.4z High-Rate Pulse Repetition Frequency (HRP)" ranging, which made pairs of Apple U1 chips, and U1 chips working with NXP and Qorvo UWB chips (chip families also used for car entry), report 0 m when the devices were 12 m apart, with success probabilities up to 4% and a device costing about USD 65. Distance bounding is only as strong as the receiver's handling of the physical signal.

**A different weakness: weak fob cryptography.** In 2018 researchers at COSIC, an imec group at KU Leuven, showed that the Pektron PKES system used on the Tesla Model S relied on **DST40**, a proprietary cipher whose key had already been shown too short in 2005. NVD's entry [CVE-2018-16806](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-16806) records the method: "a 5.4 TB precomputation, followed by wake-frame reception and two challenge/response operations, to clone a key fob within a few seconds". They reported to Tesla on 31 August 2017; Tesla paid a USD 10,000 bounty and added options to disable passive entry and require a PIN to drive ([imec release](https://www.imec-int.com/en/articles/security-flaws-in-passive-keyless-entry-and-start-systems)). Relay attacks borrow the real key; this attack *copied* it.

**Defender view.** Immediate measures from the ETH paper: shield the key in a metal case (a Faraday cage) when not in use, or a software option to switch passive entry off, both at a cost in convenience. Engineering measures: UWB ranging with careful receiver design, modern ciphers with full-length keys, PIN-to-drive, and logging of unlock and start events so that a theft investigation can see when the car believed its key was present. Note that the ETH team points out a relay attack leaves "no physical traces of car entry", so only the car's own logs can show what happened.

blocks.question: A maker upgrades its PKES fob from a 40-bit cipher to AES-128. Does this stop relay attacks?
options: Yes, because the relay cannot decrypt AES
Yes, if the challenge is longer
No, because the relay forwards the genuine key's signals and never needs to understand them; only proximity checks stop it
No, because AES is also 40-bit in fobs
blocks.explain: The relay is protocol-independent. Stronger cryptography fixes cloning attacks like the DST40 case, but the car still receives a valid response from the real key. Only measuring distance (or the owner disabling passive entry) addresses relaying.

blocks.question: Why do round-trip timeouts of 35 microseconds give no relay protection?
options: Because radio is slower than light
Because 35 microseconds lets a signal travel about 10.5 km, so any practical relay fits inside it
Because the key's processing time is longer than 35 microseconds
Because LF signals cannot be timed
blocks.explain: Distance bounding needs nanosecond resolution: 1 ns is about 30 cm. A window of tens of microseconds was set for protocol timing, not distance.

lessons.title: Case: CAN injection theft through a headlight, 2023

blocks.md:
In 2022 Ian Tabor, an automotive cybersecurity researcher, found the front bumper and headlight wiring of a Toyota RAV4 they owned pulled apart, twice. Days after the second time the car was stolen. Tabor investigated with Noel Lowdon of the vehicle forensics firm Harper Shaw, and Ken Tindell of Canis Automotive Labs analysed the CAN side and published it on 3 April 2023 ([CAN Injection: keyless car theft](https://kentindell.github.io/2023/04/03/can-injection/)). Tabor also found a website selling the tool as an "emergency start" device, at prices up to EUR 5000. It is the CAN-has-no-authentication lesson turned into a product.

Tiny example of the idea: the smart key receiver ECU normally announces on the bus that a valid key is present. If something else announces the same thing, nothing on the bus can tell the difference.

What happened, at the level of mechanism:

1. **Access**: pulling back the bumper exposes the headlight connector, which carries the control CAN bus. The smart key receiver ECU is connected to that same bus, and on the RAV4 the headlight was the easiest place to reach it from outside.
2. **Silencing**: the device's modified CAN transceiver overrides the bus so that no other device can drive a dominant bit; other ECUs' frames fail and they go through CAN error recovery. The car logged many fault codes (DTCs, diagnostic trouble codes) showing lost communication with the lighting ECU and other systems.
3. **Impersonation**: the device sent frames equivalent to "key validated, unlock immobilizer", as if from the smart key receiver.
4. **Forwarding**: the gateway ECU copied those frames to the powertrain bus, where the engine ECU accepted them and released the immobiliser. A further frame told the door ECU to unlock.

The hardware was hidden in the case of a Bluetooth speaker. A neighbour's Toyota Land Cruiser was stolen soon after.

blocks.title: CAN injection: one bus reached from outside, trust copied inward

scenes.caption: Normal: the smart key receiver checks the key by radio and announces "key valid" on the control CAN bus. The gateway forwards it to the engine ECU.
Access: the thief reaches the same bus at the headlight connector, outside the locked cabin.
Silencing: dominant override holds other nodes off the bus; their frames fail and fault codes are logged.
Impersonation: the injector sends "key validated". The gateway cannot tell it from the real receiver and forwards it; the engine ECU unlocks the immobiliser.
A second injected frame unlocks the doors. Nothing was hacked in software; the network simply believed a frame.

blocks.md:
Tindell proposed two levels of fix. A **quick fix** in software: the gateway "could be re-programmed to only forward a smart key CAN frame if it has recently transmitted a CAN frame without problems", since this injector necessarily disturbs the bus (quoting Ian Fleming: "Once is happenstance, twice is coincidence, and three times is enemy action"). The **real fix** is cryptographic, a "Zero Trust" approach in which ECUs require proof that messages are genuine, for example with a software-emulated SHE (lesson 9), unique keys per vehicle, and the bus overhead of authentication tags.

The code compares the three gateway policies on the owner's normal unlock and on the thief's sequence.

blocks.caption: Toy gateway policies. "quiet bus" is in the spirit of Tindell's quick fix, not a real product's logic; "mac" stands for a SecOC-style check.

blocks.code:
forward all | owner:
  t=0: forwarded to powertrain bus
forward all | thief:
  t=120: forwarded to powertrain bus
quiet bus | owner:
  t=0: forwarded to powertrain bus
quiet bus | thief:
  t=120: DROPPED, bus errors 80 ms ago; log event
mac | owner:
  t=0: forwarded to powertrain bus
mac | thief:
  t=120: DROPPED, authenticator check failed; log event
blocks.caption: Output of the code above (a real run).

blocks.md:
Read the trade-off in the output. The heuristic stops this exact injector but relies on the attacker disturbing the bus; a better injector that waits for a quiet moment would pass. The authenticator check stops any sender without the key, whatever its timing, but needs keys provisioned per vehicle and room in the frame (lesson 4).

**Defender view.** Prevention: authenticate security-critical frames such as key validation and immobiliser release end to end (SecOC from the smart key receiver to the engine ECU), and do not route them over buses that are reachable from outside the cabin. Detection: a burst of communication fault codes on a parked car, followed by a start, is exactly the IDS signal of lessons 3 and 5. Response: the fix is a software update to many ECUs, the case for secure OTA (lesson 10).

It is tempting to call this a physical attack and declare it out of scope: "if they can pull off the bumper, they can do anything". The thieves needed no key, no tools beyond a disguised gadget, and a few minutes outside the car. Threat models must include every wire reachable without entering the vehicle.

blocks.question: Why did the gateway forward the thieves' "key validated" frame to the engine ECU?
options: The gateway forwards that identifier by design, and on plain CAN it cannot tell an injected frame from the smart key receiver's
The thieves reprogrammed the gateway
The frame carried a valid SecOC tag
The engine ECU was on the same bus as the headlight
blocks.explain: Forwarding by identifier is the gateway's job. Without an authenticator, the injected frame is byte-for-byte what the genuine receiver would send. The case write-up describes the gateway copying the frame to the powertrain bus.

blocks.question: Tindell's quick fix forwards a smart key frame only if the gateway has recently transmitted a frame without problems. What is its main weakness?
options: It blocks the owner's genuine key
It needs AES hardware
It only works on CAN FD
An attacker who can inject without causing errors (for example, when the genuine ECU is silent) is not detected
blocks.explain: The heuristic keys on a side effect of this particular injector. That makes it a good fast mitigation and a poor final answer, which is why the write-up pairs it with cryptographic authentication.

lessons.title: The cloud is part of the car: connected-car API failures

blocks.md:
Every remote feature, such as unlocking from a phone app, needs a backend that sends commands to the car's telematics unit. That backend is also reached by dealer portals, fleet tools and partners. If any of them can issue commands for a car it should not control, the attacker does not need to touch the vehicle at all. The IoT course made the same point with the Verkada case: the maker's cloud is part of the device.

Tiny example: a dealer website lets staff add a new owner to a car after a sale. If the site checks only that you are logged in as *some* dealer, not that this car is one of *your* sales, anyone who can become a dealer can take over any car.

That pattern has a name in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (OWASP: Open Worldwide Application Security Project): [API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/), BOLA. An API checks *who you are* but not whether *this object* (this VIN, this account) is yours.

In January 2023 Sam Curry, a web security researcher, and colleagues (Neiko Rivera, Brett Buerhaus, Maik Robert, Ian Carroll, Justin Rhinehart and Shubham Shah) published "Web Hackers vs. The Auto Industry" ([summary](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2023/01/security-vulnerabilities-in-major-car-brands-revealed)). The write-up (unlinked: it shows the requests) reports remote control and account takeover "via VIN" at Kia, Honda, Infiniti, Nissan and Acura; via owner email at Hyundai and Genesis; single sign-on flaws exposing staff tools at BMW, Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Benz; and leaked AWS keys at SiriusXM. A VIN (vehicle identification number) is printed on the windscreen: it identifies a car, it does not authorise anyone to control it.

**Case: the Kia dealer portal, 2024.** Neiko Rivera, Sam Curry, Justin Rhinehart, Ian Carroll and Kenneth Lugo found that the Kia Connect dealer site exposed dealer-only API functions (write-up "Hacking Kia", not linked; [news summary](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2024/09/millions-of-kia-vehicles-were-vulnerable-to-remote-attacks-with-just-a-license-plate-number)). What broke: anyone could register an account that received a session with dealer functions, and those functions looked up a car by VIN (which third-party services derive from a licence plate), returned the owner's contact details, and could add another account as the car's primary owner, with no check that this dealer had anything to do with this car.

The result, per the write-up: tracking and commands such as "unlock, start, or honk" in "about 30 seconds", on Kia vehicles built after 2013, with or without a Kia Connect subscription. Timeline: reported 11 June 2024; Kia reported the fix 14 August; disclosed late September 2024. The researchers state that Kia "validated this was never exploited maliciously".

blocks.title: BOLA in a dealer API: logged in is not the same as allowed

scenes.caption: A self-registered dealer account gets a valid session token. Authentication succeeded, correctly: this is a real account.
The account asks for a car's owner by VIN. The API checks the token, not whether this dealer handles this car.
It then makes itself the primary owner. Again only the token is checked. No message reaches the real owner.
Owner-level commands now flow through the normal telematics path to the car. The car does exactly what it was designed to do.

blocks.code:
# A dealer API that reassigns a connected car's owner (toy model).
VEHICLES = {"VIN123": {"owner": "ana@example.com", "dealer": "D-7"}}
SESSIONS = {"tok-real": {"dealer": "D-7", "verified": True},
            "tok-self": {"dealer": "D-99", "verified": False}}  # self-registered
NOTIFY = []

def set_owner_v1(token, vin, email):
    s = SESSIONS.get(token)
    if not s:                                   # authenticated? yes. authorised?
        return "401"
    VEHICLES[vin]["owner"] = email              # never asked
    return "200 owner changed"

def set_owner_v2(token, vin, email, sale_record=None):
    s = SESSIONS.get(token)
    if not s or not s["verified"]:
        return "403 dealer account not verified"
    car = VEHICLES.get(vin)
    if not car or car["dealer"] != s["dealer"]:
        return "403 vehicle not handled by this dealer"   # object-level check
    if not sale_record:
        return "409 no completed sale for this VIN"
    NOTIFY.append((car["owner"], f"Owner change for {vin} requested"))
    car["owner"] = email
    return "200 owner changed; previous owner notified"

print("v1 self-registered:", set_owner_v1("tok-self", "VIN123", "x@evil.test"))
VEHICLES["VIN123"]["owner"] = "ana@example.com"          # reset the demo
print("v2 self-registered:", set_owner_v2("tok-self", "VIN123", "x@evil.test"))
print("v2 real dealer, no sale:", set_owner_v2("tok-real", "VIN123", "b@example.com"))
print("v2 real dealer, sale:", set_owner_v2("tok-real", "VIN123", "b@example.com", "S-881"))
print("notifications:", NOTIFY)
blocks.caption: Toy model of the pattern, not Kia's code (which is not public). v1 authenticates; v2 also authorises the object and notifies the owner.

blocks.code:
v1 self-registered: 200 owner changed
v2 self-registered: 403 dealer account not verified
v2 real dealer, no sale: 409 no completed sale for this VIN
v2 real dealer, sale: 200 owner changed; previous owner notified
notifications: [('ana@example.com', 'Owner change for VIN123 requested')]
blocks.caption: Output of the code above (a real run).

blocks.md:
Why v2 works: it rejects accounts that were never verified as dealers; it checks that *this* VIN belongs to *this* dealer (object-level authorisation, the actual BOLA fix); it requires evidence of a sale before an ownership change; and it tells the previous owner, which turns a silent takeover into a visible one.

Two more cases show other backend failure classes:

- **Subaru, November 2024**: in their write-up "Hacking Subaru" (January 2025, not linked), Sam Curry and Shubham Shah report that the STARLINK admin portal's password-reset endpoint reset employee accounts without a confirmation token, and its second factor was enforced only in the browser. Access gave remote start, lock and unlock, and a year of location history "accurate to within 5 meters". Their timeline puts the fix about 16 hours after the report ([Carscoops](https://www.carscoops.com/2025/01/subaru-starlink-flaw-could-have-let-hackers-unlock-and-track-millions-of-drivers/): within 24 hours).

**Toyota T-Connect, 2022**: a subcontractor published part of the T-Connect site's source code, including an access key to a customer-data server, in a public GitHub repository in December 2017. It was found on 15 September 2022; 296,019 email addresses and customer numbers were exposed; Toyota made the repository private at once and changed the key two days later ([The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2022/10/11/toyota_source_code_email_leak/)).

**Defender view.** UN R155 Annex 5 starts with back-end threats: "Abuse of privileges by staff (insider attack)" and "Unauthorized internet access to the server". The controls are ordinary web security applied with fleet-scale consequences: object-level authorisation on every endpoint that takes a VIN or account ID; verified onboarding for dealer and partner accounts; server-side enforcement of every authentication factor; secret scanning in code repositories; and monitoring that alerts on ownership changes, a single account touching many VINs, or remote commands to cars far from the account's usual pattern. Each command a car receives should be traceable to an authorised human or service.

blocks.question: An API endpoint `POST /vehicles/{vin}/unlock` requires a valid owner session token. Which test best checks for BOLA?
options: Send the request with no token
Send the request with owner A's valid token for a VIN that belongs to owner B
Send a malformed VIN
Send the request twice quickly
blocks.explain: BOLA is about the object, not the login. A valid token for the wrong object is exactly the case a missing ownership check lets through; the other tests probe authentication, input validation and rate limiting.

blocks.question: In the Subaru case, what did enforcing the second factor only in the browser mean?
options: The second factor was secure because browsers are sandboxed
The second factor was sent by SMS
The server did not require the second factor, so a client that skipped the browser's prompt still had access
Employees had to use a hardware key
blocks.explain: Any check that runs only in the client can be skipped by a client that behaves differently. The write-up describes bypassing the prompt by removing a client-side overlay; the server must enforce every factor.

lessons.title: EV charging: ISO 15118 Plug and Charge and OCPP

blocks.md:
Charging an electric vehicle (EV) involves more parties than filling a tank, and each link is a network protocol:

- **EV to charging station**: ISO 15118, which carries **Plug and Charge**: the car identifies its charging contract by certificate, with no card or app.
- **Charging station to its operator's backend**: **OCPP** (Open Charge Point Protocol), run by a **CPO** (charge point operator) whose backend is the **CSMS** (charging station management system).
- **Contracts and billing**: an **eMSP** (e-mobility service provider) sells the driver a charging contract usable at many CPOs.

Tiny example: you plug in at a motorway charger you have never used. Within seconds charging starts and the bill reaches your eMSP. For that, the station must trust the car's contract, the car must trust the station, and the station must trust commands from a CSMS somewhere on the internet.

Plug and Charge rests on a public-key infrastructure (PKI), described by Adrian Kailus, Dustin Kern and Christoph Krauss ([arXiv 2403.06632](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06632)). It has four parts, each with up to two sub-CAs under a root:

- **CPO PKI**: certificates for charging stations, used to authenticate the station in TLS. Its root is the **V2G root CA** (V2G: vehicle-to-grid).
- **OEM PKI** (original equipment manufacturer): the carmaker's **provisioning certificate** in each car, with a unique Provisioning Certificate Identifier (PCID): the car's initial trust anchor for installing contract credentials. Under ISO 15118-20 the OEM also issues a **vehicle certificate** for TLS.
- **eMSP PKI**: issues the **contract certificate** (with a unique contract ID, the eMAID, e-Mobility Account Identifier) and its private key. That private key is encrypted with the public key of the car's provisioning certificate, so only that car can use it.
- **CPS PKI** (certificate provisioning service): signs the contract data, chaining to the V2G root, so the car need not know every eMSP's root.
The first edition, ISO 15118-2, authenticates only the station in TLS and the car by challenge-response inside the tunnel; ISO 15118-20 uses mutual TLS with the vehicle certificate.

blocks.title: Plug and Charge: whose certificate proves what

scenes.caption: TLS first: the charging station presents a certificate from the CPO PKI, which chains to the V2G root that the car trusts.
The car was built with an OEM provisioning certificate. When a contract is first installed, the contract's private key arrives encrypted to that certificate's public key.
The eMSP creates the contract certificate; the CPS signs the package under the V2G root. The car verifies up to the V2G root without knowing the eMSP's own root.
Charging: the car proves its contract to the station; the station reports to its operator's CSMS over OCPP, ideally on mutually authenticated TLS (profile 3).

blocks.md:
Real deployments struggle with the TLS layer. CharIN (Charging Interface Initiative), an EV charging industry association, published a [guide in April 2026](https://www.charin.global/media/pages/technology/knowledge-base/03858ecdca-1779802496/20260418_charin_implementation_guide_for_tls_with_iso_15118_-_avoidance_and_handling_of_wrong_implementations_-2.pdf) because "ISO 15118-2 requires TLS 1.2 for Plug & Charge, while ISO 15118-20 requires TLS 1.3 with mutual authentication": cars now offer both versions, many chargers implement only -2 with libraries that pick TLS 1.3 by default, and handshakes fail. CharIN recommends TLS 1.2 only for -2 and TLS 1.3 only for -20. (TLS 1.3 is now RFC 9846.)

Long-lived roots raise a planning question. NIST's [IR 8547](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8547/final) deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve signatures after 2030 and disallows them after 2035, while cars and chargers bought today will still be in service then. V2G, OEM and eMSP PKIs need a migration path to post-quantum signatures.

**OCPP security profiles**, from the Open Charge Alliance's [Security Operations Guide](https://openchargealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/ocpp_security_operations_guide-2.pdf) (January 2026):

- **Profile 1**, basic authentication over unsecured transport, "by itself is not secure": no CSMS authentication, no secure channel. It exists for networks where a VPN protects the link, and a CPO "SHALL NOT use this in untrusted networks".
- **Profile 2**, TLS with HTTP basic authentication: OCPP requires a password of at least 16 characters, and the CSMS must watch for brute force of station ID and password.
- **Profile 3**, TLS with client-side certificates on both ends.

OCPP 2.x without profile 2 "is NOT considered a valid OCPP 2.x implementation". Downgrades are restricted: never to profile 1, from 3 to 2 only if a setting allows it, and once it connects with a higher profile it deletes its lower-profile connection settings, so an attacker who disrupts the link cannot force a fallback. A CSMS "SHALL NOT accept unknown Charging Station IDs" during provisioning.

blocks.caption: Toy CSMS admission policy implementing the guide's rules: no profile 1 on untrusted networks, no downgrade, 16-character minimum, unknown IDs rejected.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** A charger is an internet-connected device on a street corner. The OCPP guide treats tampering with stations "in the field" and stolen SIM cards as realistic; it advises not running local interfaces or OCPP services as root, and not shipping well-known root CA bundles, because the station should trust only its own PKI. For the backend, the CSMS is the high-value target: one compromise reaches every station. Monitor station identities, failed logins, firmware update commands and unusual remote stop or start patterns across the fleet.

blocks.question: Under ISO 15118 Plug and Charge, why is the contract certificate's private key encrypted to the car's OEM provisioning certificate?
options: So that only the specific car holding the matching provisioning private key can install and use the contract credentials
To compress it
Because the charging station needs to read it
Because TLS 1.2 requires it
blocks.explain: The eMSP generates the key pair, so it must deliver the private key securely. Encrypting it to the provisioning certificate's public key binds it to one vehicle, as Kailus, Kern and Krauss describe.

blocks.question: A charging station has connected with security profile 3. Its connection is then disrupted, and on reconnect it is offered only profile 1. What should happen under OCPP's rules?
options: Accept profile 1 temporarily to keep charging available
Refuse: a station that connected with a higher profile removes lower-profile settings and must not fall back, and the CSMS must not accept the lower profile either
Accept profile 2 but not 1, with no other condition
Use profile 1 if the password is 16 characters
blocks.explain: The guide says stations remove lower-profile connection profiles after connecting with a higher one, so "a Charging Station SHALL thus not fall back", and the CSMS must refuse the lower profile. Allowing a fallback would let any network disruption become a downgrade attack.

lessons.title: UN R155, R156 and ISO/SAE 21434: risk assessment by the numbers

blocks.md: **UN Regulation 155** (UN R155) is a United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) vehicle regulation, adopted in Geneva on 24 June 2020 and in force since 22 January 2021; the [UN treaty record](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/MTDSG/Volume%20I/Chapter%20XI/XI-B-16-155.en.xml) lists 59 parties applying it, including the EU, Japan, the Republic of Korea and the UK. It covers vehicles of categories L, M, N and O "fitted with at least one electronic control unit" ([consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/5/oj/eng/pdf)). The EU made it mandatory through its General Safety Regulation ([Regulation (EU) 2019/2144](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/2144/oj/eng/pdf)), Annex II row D4 "Protection of vehicle against cyberattacks": type approval refused for new types from 6 July 2022, and registration of non-compliant new vehicles prohibited from 7 July 2024.

Tiny example of what it demands: before a new model can be approved, the maker must show a risk assessment that considered every threat in R155's Annex 5 (CAN messages, diagnostics, back-end servers, updates) and the mitigations chosen for each.

R155 has two layers:

- **CSMS** (cyber security management system, not lesson 14's charging CSMS): the organisation's processes, certified by an approval authority. The certificate "shall remain valid for a maximum of three years". Processes must cover risk identification and treatment, testing, supplier risks, and to "monitor for, detect and respond to cyber-attacks", including vehicles after first registration, with reports to the authority "at least once a year".
- **Vehicle type**: for each model, the maker must "perform an exhaustive risk assessment", treat the risks with "Proportionate mitigations", include every relevant mitigation from Annex 5 Parts B and C (or justify an alternative), test before approval, and use cryptographic modules "in line with consensus standards".

Its companion **UN R156** (lesson 10) does the same for software updates. R155 says what must be achieved, not how. The industry method is the standard **ISO/SAE 21434** (Road vehicles: Cybersecurity engineering), developed jointly by ISO and SAE International from 2016 and released in August 2021.

The core of ISO/SAE 21434 is **TARA** (threat analysis and risk assessment). Its steps, as summarised by Abouelnaga and Jakobs ([arXiv 2307.02261](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02261)):

1. **Asset identification**: what has value, and which property (integrity, confidentiality, availability) matters. Example: the "key validated" frame; integrity.
2. **Damage scenarios**: what harm a compromise causes. Example: car driven away by a thief.
3. **Impact rating** in four categories, safety, financial, operational and privacy, each **severe, major, moderate or negligible** (safety ratings derived from ISO 26262, the functional safety standard).
4. **Threat scenarios** and **attack path analysis** (attack trees, or bottom-up from vulnerabilities).
5. **Attack feasibility**: high, medium, low or very low.
6. **Risk value** from 1 (minimum) to 5 (maximum), from impact and feasibility.
7. **Risk treatment**: avoid, reduce, share or transfer, or retain, per the fortiss white paper ([arXiv 2012.15080](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15080)).

blocks.title: ISO/SAE 21434 example risk matrix (impact by feasibility)

scenes.caption: Risk values 1 to 5. Rows: impact. Columns: attack feasibility. Severe impact never drops below 2, however hard the attack.
Design phase, before tools exist: spoofing the key-validated frame takes an expert about a month with restricted knowledge. Potential 18, medium feasibility, severe impact: risk 4.
After a ready-made injector is sold to thieves: a layman, within a day, public know-how. Potential 5, high feasibility: risk 5. The same threat moved because the world changed.
With per-vehicle keys and authenticated key frames, a forger needs bespoke work and secret knowledge: potential 46, very low feasibility, risk 2.

blocks.caption: Attack potential factor values and feasibility bands as reproduced by Unger et al. (2023); the scenario ratings are this course's illustration.

blocks.code:
design phase: first discovery            potential 18 -> medium   x severe   = risk 4
after a device is sold to thieves        potential  5 -> high     x severe   = risk 5
same, with authenticated key frames      potential 46 -> very low x severe   = risk 2

blocks.md:
Two lessons hide in that output. First, TARA ratings are **judgements that expire**: the second row is the same threat as the first after tooling appeared, which is why R155 requires continual monitoring and why a TARA must be revisited when incidents happen elsewhere. Second, the treatment changed *feasibility*, not *impact*: theft stays severe, so risk can fall only to 2. Whether 2 is acceptable is a risk-treatment decision that should be documented along with who made it.

The fortiss white paper's worked example is a headlamp system whose body controller sends on/off requests over CAN, with a gateway separating it from a navigation ECU with cellular and Bluetooth interfaces. In 2023, thieves used exactly a headlamp's CAN connection; a TARA that rated the headlamp bus as low-value would have missed that it also carried key validation.

A TARA done once for type approval and filed away satisfies nobody. R155's vehicle-type rules require mitigations for the risks identified, its CSMS rules require responses to new threats "within a reasonable timeframe", and attack feasibility drops every time a tool is published or sold.

blocks.question: Using the example values, an attack needs up to 1 week (1), a proficient attacker (3), restricted knowledge (3), easy window (1) and specialized equipment (4). Its impact is major. What is the risk value?
blocks.explain: Potential = 1+3+3+1+4 = 12, which is 13 or less, so feasibility is high. Major impact with high feasibility gives 4 in the example matrix. A common slip is to treat a low potential score as low feasibility; it is the reverse.

blocks.question: Which statement about UN R155 is correct?
options: It requires a certified cyber security management system and a per-type risk assessment covering Annex 5 threats, plus continual monitoring after sale
It prescribes specific algorithms such as AES-128 CMAC for CAN
It applies only to electric vehicles
It replaces ISO/SAE 21434
blocks.explain: R155 sets outcomes and processes: CSMS certification (valid up to three years), an exhaustive risk assessment per vehicle type, Annex 5 mitigations and monitoring with yearly reporting. It asks for consensus-standard cryptography without naming algorithms, and ISO/SAE 21434 is the usual method for meeting it.

lessons.title: A secure vehicle end to end, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Put the course together as one design. No single control would have stopped every case you studied; each case was stopped, or would have been, by a different layer. That is the argument for defence in depth in a car: the layers fail independently, so an attacker must break several.

Tiny example: the 2023 CAN injection needed physical access to a bus, an unauthenticated key frame, and a gateway willing to forward it. Authenticating that one frame breaks the chain even if the other two remain.

blocks.title: Layers of a defended vehicle, from cloud to CAN frame

scenes.caption: Backend: object-level authorisation, verified partner onboarding, secret scanning, monitoring of ownership changes (Kia, Subaru, Toyota cases).
Connectivity: no inbound listeners on telematics and head units; carrier-side filtering; signed updates with split trust (Jeep, Uptane).
Gateways and zones: forward only what each source needs; diagnostics only from the OBD path, authenticated, while stationary.
In-vehicle network: SecOC on security- and safety-critical signals; IDS rules for timing, unknown IDs and error bursts (CAN injection, bus-off).
ECU: secure boot that locks keys, per-ECU secrets in SHE or an HSM, debug ports locked (IoT course), modern ciphers in key fobs.
Around all of it: security events flow to a vehicle SOC, and R155 processes turn incidents into updated TARAs and OTA fixes.

blocks.code:
# Each real case as a chain of steps; a control "breaks" a step.
CASES = {
    "Jeep 2015":          ["reach head unit over cellular", "run code on head unit",
                           "reflash CAN chip unsigned", "send frames to safety ECUs"],
    "CAN injection 2023": ["reach CAN wires at headlamp", "silence real ECU",
                           "fake key-validated frame", "gateway forwards it"],
    "Kia portal 2024":    ["register as dealer", "look up car by VIN",
                           "add self as owner", "send remote commands"],
    "PKES relay":         ["relay LF/UHF radio", "car accepts long round trip"],
}
CONTROLS = {
    "no inbound ports / carrier filtering": {"reach head unit over cellular"},
    "signed ECU firmware":                  {"reflash CAN chip unsigned"},
    "gateway allow-list":                   {"send frames to safety ECUs"},
    "error-aware gateway (heuristic)":      {"silence real ECU"},
    "SecOC on key/safety frames":           {"fake key-validated frame", "send frames to safety ECUs"},
    "object-level authorisation + notify":  {"add self as owner"},
    "verified dealer onboarding":           {"register as dealer"},
    "UWB distance bounding":                {"car accepts long round trip"},
}
for case, steps in CASES.items():
    hits = [c for c, s in CONTROLS.items() if s & set(steps)]
    print(f"{case:19} broken by {len(hits)}: {', '.join(hits)}")
blocks.caption: Each case as a chain of steps; count the controls from this course that break at least one step.

Jeep 2015           broken by 4: no inbound ports / carrier filtering, signed ECU firmware, gateway allow-list, SecOC on key/safety frames
CAN injection 2023  broken by 2: error-aware gateway (heuristic), SecOC on key/safety frames
Kia portal 2024     broken by 2: object-level authorisation + notify, verified dealer onboarding
PKES relay          broken by 1: UWB distance bounding

blocks.md:
The output makes the depth visible. The Jeep chain had four separate places to break; the relay attack has essentially one technical fix (distance bounding) plus the owner's own behaviour; the Kia chain is pure backend. When you review a vehicle design, write the chains for its likely attacks and check that each has at least two independent breaks, then turn those into TARA treatments and test cases.

**The legal line.** Test only vehicles, ECUs, accounts and services you own or have written permission to test. The connected-car researchers in this course reported to the makers first, and in the Kia and Subaru cases published only after the fixes were confirmed; that is the model to follow. Where a maker publishes a vulnerability disclosure policy, it tells you what testing is authorised and how to report.

**Where to practise legally, on your own machine:**

- Linux's **SocketCAN** stack includes a virtual CAN driver, `vcan`; its virtual interfaces "allow the transmission and reception of CAN frames without real CAN controller hardware" ([kernel CAN guide](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/can.html)). On a Linux machine or VM you can create a virtual bus and run this course's IDS and SecOC ideas against your own simulated ECUs, with no car attached.
- The [HCRL car-hacking dataset](https://ocslab.hksecurity.net/Datasets/car-hacking-dataset) gives real logged traffic with labelled DoS, fuzzing and spoofing injections: a good test set for the timing and allowlist detector from lesson 5.
- AUTOSAR's SecOC, Dcm and SHE specifications are free to read; they are the documents much production ECU software is built to.
- For broader skills (cryptography, web API testing, reverse engineering), [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/), Carnegie Mellon's free security education programme and capture-the-flag practice.

Cars fail where trust is assumed: CAN trusts every sender, keyless entry trusts that radio means proximity, dealer APIs trust any logged-in dealer, and gateways trust identifiers. Every control in this course replaces one assumption with a check: a MAC, a signature, a timed exchange, an object-level authorisation.

blocks.question: A team must choose one control to add first to a car whose key-validation frame travels unauthenticated over a bus exposed at the headlights. Which gives the most direct protection against the 2023 attack?
options: Encrypting the telematics link
Moving the OBD-II port
SecOC-style authentication of the key-validation frame with per-vehicle keys, checked by the ECU that releases the immobiliser
A longer UDS seed
blocks.explain: The attack's decisive step is a forged key-validation frame. Authenticating that frame end to end defeats it whatever bus the thief reaches. The other controls address different chains.

blocks.question: Why count "independent breaks" per attack chain rather than total controls?
options: Because regulators require exactly two
Because several controls that all depend on the same assumption (for example, all trusting the gateway) fail together, giving less depth than their number suggests
Because each control costs the same
Because attackers only ever use one step
blocks.explain: Defence in depth works when layers fail for different reasons. Two filters in the same gateway are one break if the gateway is compromised; a gateway rule plus a MAC checked at the receiver are two.
